papers.title: Beyond psychedelic exceptionalism: how people combine meditation with psychoactive substances, and how this relates to well-being.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Combining meditation with psychoactive substances is often assumed to be a niche practice centred on classic psychedelics. We sought to broaden this narrative in two cross-sectional studies. METHODS: Study 1 used a broad naturalistic sample (N = 1,391) to examine the prevalence of substance use, meditation, and their simultaneous combination, as well as associations with subjective happiness. Study 2 used a stratified subsample (n = 397) focusing on classic psychedelic and cannabis users, the most common psychedelic-type substances combined with meditation, to assess associations with mental well-being, peace of mind, psychological flexibility, depression, and anxiety. RESULTS: Contrary to prevailing assumptions, alcohol (29%), cannabis (19%), and nicotine (16%) were far more commonly combined with meditation than classic psychedelics (6%). Classic psychedelic use was also embedded within a pattern of pronounced polysubstance use, suggesting that it may reflect a broader substance-use profile rather than an isolated behavioural practice. Regression analyses found no consistent associations between psychedelic or cannabis use, with or without meditation, and any outcome. However, an unexpected pattern emerged for other drugs and alcohol. Other- drug use without meditation was associated with poorer well-being outcomes relative to no other-drug use, whereas other-drug use combined with meditation was not. Alcohol combined with meditation was associated with better well-being outcomes relative to alcohol use without meditation. CONCLUSIONS: These findings suggest that combining meditation with substance use is not limited to psychedelics and should be studied within broader patterns of polysubstance use and meditation practice.

papers.title: Interdisciplinary Weight Management in a Safety-Net Health System: A Pilot Implementation Study.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Despite the high prevalence of obesity and cardiometabolic diseases in safety-net populations, access to intensive, evidence-based lifestyle interventions and scalable implementation strategies remains limited. This study evaluated the effectiveness, acceptability, and feasibility of an interdisciplinary program in an urban safety-net health system. METHODS: This single-center, mixed-methods implementation evaluation assessed LA VIDA, a 6-month interdisciplinary weight management program for medically complex individuals. Outcomes included feasibility, patient engagement, self-rated health, quality of life, physical activity, dietary behaviors, and program satisfaction. RESULTS: Over 2 years, 95 participants completed the program. They were predominantly female (72.6%) and Latino (78.9%), with a mean age of 50 years, median BMI of 39.2 (IQR: 36.9 to 43.7), and 60% having ≥ 3 comorbidities. Median 6-month weight loss was 5.5% (IQR: -2.6% to -9.9%), with significant improvements in quality of life (p = 0.0003), physical health (p < 0.0001), moderate-intensity physical activity (p < 0.001), and dietary behaviors. Participants reported high satisfaction driven by personalized guidance, increased health knowledge, mindfulness, and the supportive group environment. CONCLUSIONS: LA VIDA was feasible and acceptable and improved patient-reported behaviors and outcomes in a safety-net setting. These findings support it as an effective model for integrated obesity care that combines lifestyle, behavioral, and pharmacologic treatment in the safety net.

papers.title: Orbitofrontal-ventral striatal coupling: A model of the neurobehavioral architecture of craving in substance use disorders.
papers.abstract: Neuroimaging has identified cue-elicited activity in ventral striatum and orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) as a reliable signature of craving, yet activation magnitude in either region is an inconsistent predictor of clinical outcome. This theoretical review develops a model on which the clinically consequential variable is not activation but effective coupling: the cue-evoked gain-the factor by which an input is amplified-with which OFC valuation signals modulate ventral striatal action-selection activity. I formalize this gain as valuation-policy coupling (λ), which governs the probability that a drug-related appraisal recruits approach and consumption policies; it is a latent construct indexed by effective OFC-accumbens connectivity, approach bias under load, and pharmacological challenge. Two moderators-meta-awareness and elaborative versus nonelaborative engagement-determine whether the urge is re-entered or exited, and jointly specify a neurocognitive space in which craving occupies a high-λ, high-meta-awareness, elaborative vertex. The framework predicts an awareness-amplification effect-noticing an urge intensifies it under high λ and weakens it under low λ-specifies when mindfulness-based relapse prevention should attenuate craving and when it should not, and yields a discriminative prediction: λ-reducing interventions should reduce cue-modulated OFC-ventral-striatum coupling while leaving regional activation comparatively preserved. λ is a parameter of craving rather than of relapse-which also requires cognitive-control parameters-and a candidate transdiagnostic mechanism. Claims are labeled by evidential status; the λ-meta-awareness interaction is the model's principal hypothesis, and failure conditions are stated explicitly.

papers.title: Is Less More? Exploring the Visual Processes of Minimalist and Complex Photography Through Eye Tracking and EEG.
papers.abstract: In a world filled with an overwhelming amount of visual information, the clean and distinctive visual style of minimalist photography stands out. However, empirical research on how minimalist style affects visual cognition and psychological responses remains limited. The present study investigated the effects of photographic style (minimalist versus complex) on viewers' visual behavior, emotional responses, and brainwave state by conducting quantitative psychological experiments. Thirty participants viewed photographs in one of the two styles. Eye-tracking, consumer-grade electroencephalography (EEG), and subjective psychological assessment data were collected, enabling comprehensive evaluation of how the participants looked at, responded to, and emotionally engaged with the images. At the level of visual behavior, minimalism elicited significantly reduced number of fixations and saccades, but the duration of a single fixation is significantly longer, and the heatmap hotspots are highly concentrated, presenting a focused processing pattern of fewer but longer gazes. On a psychological level, minimalism evoked significantly less feeling of complexity and greater relaxation, although there was no significant difference in the aesthetics score between the two styles. In terms of brainwave state, viewing minimalist images resulted in significantly higher attention eSense levels, while the meditation eSense level did not show a significant difference. The results of this study therefore show that minimalist composition may influence the visual search pattern to be more focused, which is compatible with the tendency of simplified organization predicted by the principle of simplification. This study not only deepens the theoretical understanding of the psychological mechanisms of minimalist aesthetics, but also provides practical reference for visual communication and image creation of minimalist composition serving as an effective strategy for guiding the eyes toward the core subject.
